title: Parent discloses excessive sensitive identity data during registration
description: The parent sends highly sensitive personal data during account creation, including government ID alongside email, name, password, and a six-digit code. If all fields are not strictly necessary at registration time, the act of sharing creates a disclosure risk because more personal data than needed is exposed to the system.
assumptions: Assumes government ID may not be strictly necessary for initial registration or could be collected later or via a more privacy-preserving verification step.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is based on best judgement for disclosure/excessive collection; exact sub-node may vary by the project’s LINDDUN Pro tree version.

title: Registration payload can identify the parent in transit
description: The data flow contains direct identifiers and highly identifying attributes such as email, full name, and government ID. If the transmission is observable, intercepted, logged, or insufficiently protected, the payload can directly identify the parent.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may differ depending on the threat-tree version; this is a best-fit identification-in-transit threat.

title: Registration data enables linkage of the parent across contexts
description: Combining email, name, government ID, and registration metadata in one transmission can allow the parent’s identity and activity to be linked across services, records, or sessions if the flow is observed or correlated with other datasets.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit linkage node chosen; exact node numbering may vary.

title: Sensitive registration data may be disclosed in transit
description: The flow carries confidential credentials and identity data, including password and government ID. Without strong transport protection and careful handling of intermediary logs, caches, and monitoring systems, these data may be disclosed to unauthorized parties while in transit.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit disclosure node chosen; exact sub-node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Authentication service may store or process registration data in a privacy-invasive way
description: On receipt, the authentication service may retain or further process sensitive registration data such as government ID, name, email, and the six-digit code. If stored unnecessarily, logged in plaintext, or made accessible beyond need-to-know, this creates a disclosure risk at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes the service stores or logs at least part of the submitted registration payload.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node citation is approximate; selected as the closest disclosure-at-destination node.

title: Registration may collect data without sufficient necessity or consent transparency
description: The authentication service receives a broad set of personal data for registration, including government ID. If the service does not clearly justify each field, provide transparent notice, or obtain valid consent where required, the collection may violate data minimization and consent/compliance expectations.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy requirements demand necessity, transparency, and possibly consent for collecting government ID at registration.
uncertainty_note: Compliance/consent applicability depends on jurisdiction and the service’s legal basis; exact node numbering may vary.

title: Authentication service may use registration data for secondary purposes
description: Once received, the authentication service could use the parent’s registration data for purposes beyond account creation and authentication, such as profiling, analytics, or sharing with affiliates. Such secondary use would create an unawareness risk if not clearly communicated.
assumptions: Assumes potential for downstream reuse beyond the immediate registration purpose.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on actual downstream processing practices, which are not specified in the flow description.

title: Parent may be unable to prove what registration data was submitted or agreed to
description: If the authentication service does not provide adequate records, receipts, or auditable confirmation of the registration submission and associated notices, the parent may later be unable to demonstrate what personal data was provided or what terms were presented at the time.
assumptions: Assumes disputes could arise about submitted identity data, consent notices, or verification steps.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation can be less central for privacy than other threats here; included because registration often involves later disputes over submitted data and notices.

title: Excessive collection/storage of parent account data
description: The authentication service may write more parent-account personal data to the users collection than is strictly necessary for authentication and account management. Storing avoidable attributes increases privacy exposure and conflicts with data minimization.
assumptions: The 'parent account' record contains personal data beyond a minimal identifier/credential set, such as contact details, profile attributes, or other account metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimization concepts; exact subnode may differ in the canonical threat tree.

title: Over-retention of parent account data in the users collection
description: Once the parent account is stored, the users collection may retain the personal data longer than necessary for the stated purpose. Unnecessarily prolonged storage increases the chance of later disclosure or secondary use.
assumptions: MongoDB persists account records and there may be no enforced retention/deletion policy for dormant, deleted, or superseded parent accounts.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subnode for retention/storage-related disclosure is approximate.

title: Parent account data may be stored for unclear or expanded purposes
description: The destination datastore may hold parent account data in a way that enables later use beyond the original authentication purpose, such as analytics, profiling, or operational reuse, without the data subject clearly understanding those purposes.
assumptions: Purpose limitation is not technically enforced at the datastore boundary and stored records may be accessible to multiple downstream uses.
uncertainty_note: Threat depends on whether purpose limitation and transparency are enforced elsewhere; exact subnode is best-effort.

title: Storage may occur without a valid legal basis or consent handling
description: If the parent account data is written to the users collection before establishing and recording an appropriate legal basis, consent state, or other authorization for the processing, the storage operation may be non-compliant with applicable privacy obligations.
assumptions: This flow involves personal data subject to consent/legal-basis requirements and compliance evidence is not inherently guaranteed by the datastore write itself.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on jurisdiction and the actual legal basis for account creation; exact tree-node id is approximate.

title: Excessive disclosure of parent profile data in authentication response
description: The authentication service sends a JWT together with user data to the parent user. If the returned user data contains more attributes than are necessary for the immediate authentication/session-establishment purpose, the source process causes unnecessary disclosure of personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the 'user data' may include profile or account attributes beyond what is strictly needed by the parent client after login.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicable threat types/positions, not detailed node mappings.

title: JWT and response metadata can enable linkability across sessions
description: A JWT is a stable bearer artifact that may contain persistent identifiers or claims. Observers of the flow, or parties able to correlate repeated transmissions, may link multiple authentication events and associate them with the same parent user.
assumptions: Assumes the token or accompanying metadata contains stable identifiers, or that repeated transmissions are observable by an intermediary or logging component.
uncertainty_note: Applies primarily if tokens/claims are long-lived or reused and if flow metadata is observable.

title: JWT claims or accompanying user data may identify the parent user in transit
description: The authentication response may include direct identifiers (such as subject, email, account id) or indirectly identifying attributes in the JWT payload or returned user data. If exposed in transit or through intermediary inspection/logging, the parent user can be identified.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT is readable by intermediaries at some point (e.g. termination, debugging, logging) or that accompanying user data contains identifiers.
uncertainty_note: JWTs are often signed but not encrypted; exact exposure depends on transport and operational handling.

title: Parent client may detect sensitive account state from authentication response contents
description: The combination of token issuance outcome and returned user data can reveal sensitive facts to the recipient, such as role, account status, tenant membership, or other attributes not strictly necessary for using the service. This creates detectability of personal information.
assumptions: Assumes the response includes claims or fields from which sensitive states can be inferred.
uncertainty_note: This is only relevant if the returned data exposes sensitive states beyond basic login success.

title: Lack of clear notice or consent regarding returned personal data
description: If the parent user is not clearly informed that authentication will return additional user data alongside the JWT, or cannot meaningfully control that disclosure to the client application, the receipt and subsequent local processing may occur without sufficient notice/consent.
assumptions: Assumes the system returns personal data beyond what the user reasonably expects from login and that transparency/choice mechanisms are absent or weak.
uncertainty_note: Consent may not be the correct legal basis in many deployments; this threat is about insufficient notice/control rather than asserting consent is always required.

title: Credentials and parent email can identify the child account if intercepted in transit
description: The login flow carries a parent email address and password. The parent email is directly identifying, and even the combination of login metadata and account identifier can identify or single out the child account if the transmission is observable by an attacker or intermediary.
assumptions: Applies if transport confidentiality/integrity are absent, weak, or terminated in an untrusted context where the data can be observed.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include the detailed threat tree for identifiability.

title: Disclosure of parent email and password during transmission
description: The flow contains highly sensitive authentication data. If the data is sent over an insecure or improperly protected channel, the parent email and especially the password may be disclosed to network attackers, intermediaries, or logs attached to the transport path.
assumptions: Assumes the channel is not strongly protected end-to-end and that sensitive fields may be exposed in transit or transport-layer logging.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate because the detailed disclosure threat-tree nodes were not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Lack of evidence about who submitted the login request
description: If the login submission is not bound to reliable request records, the sender may later deny having initiated the login attempt, or the service may be unable to distinguish legitimate use from misuse. This can undermine accountability for privacy-relevant authentication events.
assumptions: Relevant where audit trails, timestamps, request provenance, or tamper-evident logging are insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on system logging and accountability requirements; included as a plausible but lower-confidence threat for this authentication flow.

title: Login traffic may be used to infer the child's service usage
description: Even without reading payload contents, repeated login attempts, timing, frequency, source network information, and destination metadata can allow observers to infer that a particular child account or household is using the service, revealing behavioral patterns.
assumptions: Assumes an observer can access traffic metadata such as timing, IP addresses, or endpoint information.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the detailed unawareness/non-compliance threat tree was not included in context.

title: Authentication service may expose credentials or parent email through insecure processing or storage
description: On receipt of the login data, the authentication service may disclose the parent email or password through verbose application logs, debugging traces, error reports, analytics pipelines, or improper credential handling. This creates a privacy threat at the destination element.
assumptions: Assumes the service processes or stores incoming credentials in ways that are not minimized or adequately protected.
uncertainty_note: Destination-side disclosure is strongly plausible for authentication flows, but the exact tree-node id is approximate without the detailed threat tree.

title: Collection of parent email for child login may be non-compliant if not necessary or not transparently justified
description: Using a parent email address as part of a child login can create compliance risk if the service lacks an appropriate legal basis, fails to provide clear notice, does not meet children's privacy requirements, or collects more personal data than necessary for authentication.
assumptions: Assumes the system is subject to privacy obligations concerning children and parental data, and that necessity/transparency/minimization may not be fully satisfied.
uncertainty_note: This is context-dependent on jurisdiction and product design, but it is a genuine privacy threat for a child-login flow involving parental identifiers.

title: Excessive disclosure of child profile data
description: The authentication service sends not only a JWT but also child profiles to the child user. If the returned profile set contains more attributes than are necessary for authentication or session bootstrap, the source process discloses personal data beyond the minimum needed.
assumptions: Assumes the child profiles include personal attributes and that not all included fields are strictly necessary at login.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement at a high level because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Identification of the child via JWT and profile data in transit
description: The JWT and child profile payload may directly identify the child, or enable identification when intercepted or observed in transit, especially if the token contains stable identifiers or the profiles contain names, usernames, or other identifying attributes.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT or profiles contain direct or indirect identifiers and transport/channel protections may be imperfect or observable by intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: Applies primarily if identifiers are present in token claims or profile fields.

title: Linkability through stable identifiers in token claims
description: A JWT commonly carries stable subject, account, or session-related claims. If these identifiers persist across sessions or services, observations of this flow can be linked to the same child over time or across contexts.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT contains stable identifiers such as sub, child ID, or equivalent correlatable claims.
uncertainty_note: Exact applicability depends on token design and whether identifiers are stable across contexts.

title: Local overexposure of child profiles at the recipient
description: On receipt, the child user's device or client may display, cache, or otherwise retain the child profiles in ways that expose more personal data than necessary to the child or to other users of the device.
assumptions: Assumes the external entity includes a client/device that stores or renders the received profiles.
uncertainty_note: This is a destination-side privacy threat only if the recipient environment is in scope for how received data is processed.

title: Insufficient transparency to the child about profile data returned after login
description: The child user may not understand that authentication returns both an access token and profile data, what profile attributes are included, and for what purposes they will be used locally after receipt.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly inform the child, in an age-appropriate way, about the returned data and its use.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the UX and notices presented during or after authentication.

title: Lack of demonstrable consent or lawful basis for sharing child profiles
description: Because the flow includes child profiles in addition to authentication material, the source process may share children's personal data without an appropriate consent record, parental authorization, or other lawful basis tied to this specific disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes child-profile disclosure requires a specific lawful basis beyond basic authentication and that such basis may be absent or not demonstrable.
uncertainty_note: Regulatory applicability depends on jurisdiction and system context; included because the data concerns children.

title: Excessive disclosure of child attributes during profile creation
description: The parent user may be prompted to disclose a broad set of highly sensitive child attributes at creation time (name, date of birth, gender, government ID). If all fields are collected up front without strict necessity for the immediate purpose, the act of sharing from the source causes unnecessary disclosure of the child’s personal data.
assumptions: Assumes some of these attributes may be optional or not strictly necessary at initial profile creation.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on LINDDUN disclosure/minimisation concepts; exact sub-node may differ in the canonical threat tree.

title: Identification of the child in transit via direct identifiers
description: The flow carries direct identifiers and strong identifying attributes, notably name and government ID, plus date of birth and gender. Interception or observation of this transmission could directly identify the child data subject.
assumptions: Assumes the flow is not perfectly protected end-to-end or is observable through logs, proxies, analytics, or network infrastructure.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node may vary; identification from direct identifiers clearly applies.

title: Linkability of child records through recurring identifiers and quasi-identifiers in transit
description: The combination of name, date of birth, gender, and especially government ID enables this profile-creation event to be linked with other records or transactions concerning the same child. Even if one identifier were absent elsewhere, the attribute combination can act as a strong linkage key.
assumptions: Assumes the same or overlapping attributes appear in other system flows, logs, or external datasets.
uncertainty_note: Retrieved context supports Linking generally, but exact sub-node citation is approximate.

title: Destination can link child profile data across accounts or services
description: Upon receipt, Child Profile Management can correlate the submitted child attributes with existing profiles, household accounts, historical submissions, or external verification sources. This may enable broader profiling of the child or family than the parent expects.
assumptions: Assumes P3 stores or has access to other records containing overlapping identifiers or quasi-identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the destination performs correlation beyond the immediate creation purpose.

title: Destination can identify the child uniquely from received attributes
description: The received dataset is sufficient to uniquely identify the child, especially because it includes a government ID together with name and date of birth. Identification risk arises at the destination if the system can single out the child record or associate it with a real-world identity.
assumptions: Assumes P3 stores or processes the attributes in identifiable form.

title: Destination may process more child data than necessary for profile creation
description: Child Profile Management may collect and retain government ID and other sensitive attributes even when they are not strictly necessary to create a usable child profile. This creates a data minimisation risk at the receiving process.
assumptions: Assumes government ID or some other fields are not mandatory for the stated purpose, or are retained longer than needed.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node is approximate, but the threat is a standard detectability/disclosure? No—intended here as data minimisation/non-compliance risk; if your local tree labels differ, remap accordingly.

title: Insufficient transparency or lawful basis for collecting child government ID
description: Receiving and processing a child’s government ID and other sensitive profile attributes may violate privacy obligations if the system does not provide clear notice, purpose limitation, parental authority checks, retention limits, and an appropriate lawful basis or consent mechanism.
assumptions: Assumes applicable child-data and identity-data regulations require heightened safeguards and transparency.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; non-compliance risk clearly applies given child data and government ID.

title: Parent may be unaware of downstream use of child profile attributes
description: If Child Profile Management does not clearly explain why each attribute is collected, whether government ID is mandatory, how the data will be verified, shared, or retained, the parent may be insufficiently informed about the processing of the child’s data.
assumptions: Assumes notices or just-in-time explanations are absent, unclear, or incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness often depends on UI and notice design not visible from the flow alone.

title: Excessive child-profile data written to storage
description: The Child Profile Management process may store more child personal data than is strictly necessary for profile management, such as unnecessary attributes, overly detailed free-text notes, or redundant copies of sensitive fields. This creates an avoidable disclosure because the system intentionally transfers and persists personal data beyond the minimum needed.
assumptions: The child profile contains personal data about a child and possibly guardian-linked attributes; data minimization requirements apply to the write operation.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best-fit judgement for excessive collection/storage under Data Disclosure; exact sub-node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Stored child profiles retained or exposed beyond intended purpose
description: Once received by the childprofiles collection, profile data may be stored in a way that enables avoidable disclosure, for example through indefinite retention, broad internal accessibility, or persistence of historical versions not required for the stated purpose. The privacy threat arises at the datastore because receipt and storage make the data available beyond what is necessary.
assumptions: MongoDB collection persists child profiles and may keep updates/history/backups unless explicitly controlled.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node is an approximate best fit for avoidable disclosure caused by storage/retention at destination.

title: Child records can be linked across updates and related datasets
description: Storing profile updates in a persistent collection can enable linking multiple submissions, sessions, or related records to the same child over time via stable identifiers or quasi-identifiers. This may allow construction of a richer longitudinal profile than users expect.
assumptions: Profiles are stored with stable child identifiers or combinations of attributes that permit correlation over time or with other collections.
uncertainty_note: Specific sub-node id is approximate; the threat itself is a strong fit for persistent datastore-based linkability.

title: Stored profile attributes may identify a child directly or indirectly
description: The destination collection may store direct identifiers (such as name or account id) or combinations of profile attributes that uniquely identify a child. Even if each field seems benign, the stored combination can make the child identifiable.
assumptions: Child profiles include direct identifiers or sufficiently unique combinations of demographic/profile fields.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate best fit for identifiability through stored data.

title: Profile storage may exceed or diverge from communicated consent
description: The system may write or update child profile fields in the datastore without ensuring that the stored attributes, purposes, or retention align with the consent or authorization obtained from the parent/guardian. This creates a non-compliance risk tied to the destination's processing and storage.
assumptions: Consent or another legal basis is required for at least some child-profile fields or processing purposes.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node id is approximate; applicability depends on the system's legal basis and consent design.

title: Child user directly identifies themself through account-linked interactions
description: Search requests, likes, and comments sent by the child user may contain or be bound to account identifiers, profile handles, device/account tokens, or self-disclosed personal details. By initiating these interactions, the child user may reveal identity to the service beyond what is necessary for basic content retrieval.
assumptions: Assumes the service associates requests and engagement actions with a user account, persistent identifier, or profile, and that comments may contain free-text personal information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include the detailed identification subtree.

title: Search and engagement metadata can link the child user's activities
description: Even if payload content is limited, the flow metadata and repeated requests for searches, likes, comments, and video requests can be correlated to link multiple actions to the same child user or device over time, building a behavioral profile.
assumptions: Assumes requests carry stable session, device, network, or account-related metadata that permits correlation across events.
uncertainty_note: Specific linkage subtree citation is approximate because the retrieved context did not include detailed L threat-tree nodes.

title: Video service can infer sensitive interests and behavior from interactions
description: The destination service can derive personal interests, habits, preferences, emotional state, social relationships, or potentially age-related traits from the child's searches, likes, comments, and requested videos. These inferences may exceed what the child knowingly disclosed.
assumptions: Assumes P2 logs and analyzes interaction history for recommendation, moderation, analytics, or profiling.
uncertainty_note: Detailed detectability/discoverability subtree node may differ; citation is best-effort due to missing threat-tree excerpt.

title: Secondary use of child interaction data beyond the immediate request
description: The service may use the child's search and engagement data for recommendations, personalization, analytics, advertising, model training, moderation improvement, or sharing with partners, beyond the immediate purpose of serving the requested video interaction.
assumptions: Assumes P2 retains and repurposes interaction data for secondary processing purposes.
uncertainty_note: Exact U subtree node is approximate because no detailed unlinkability tree was provided in context.

title: Improper management of children's personal data
description: Because this flow involves a child user's searches, likes, comments, and requests, the receiving service may face non-compliance risk if it collects, stores, profiles, or retains this personal data without appropriate child-specific safeguards, lawful basis/consent handling, minimization, retention limits, or transparency.
assumptions: Assumes the child is within a protected age category and the service is subject to child privacy obligations or similar data protection requirements.

title: Child may be unable to plausibly deny submitted likes or comments
description: Likes and especially comments sent from the child user's account can create attributable records tying the child to specific content or statements, reducing plausible deniability if those records are retained or exposed later.
assumptions: Assumes P2 stores engagement events with timestamps and account/device association.
uncertainty_note: Specific non-repudiation subtree citation is approximate because detailed nodes were not provided.

title: Excessive storage of video metadata and files
description: The Video Management Service may write more personal data than necessary into persistent storage, including rich video metadata and possibly full video files, creating avoidable disclosure through collection and storage beyond the minimum needed for the service purpose.
assumptions: The stored metadata or files can contain personal data about uploaders, viewers, or recorded individuals, and not all stored fields/content are strictly necessary for the stated purpose.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on general LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality structure; exact subnode may differ in the canonical threat tree.

title: Identified information embedded in video metadata
description: When the service stores video metadata, that metadata may directly identify a person, for example through uploader account identifiers, names, device identifiers, location tags, or other identifying fields attached to the video record.
assumptions: Video metadata includes fields linked to a natural person or account and these are persisted in the collection.

title: Cross-video linkability through persistent identifiers in stored records
description: By storing stable account IDs, device IDs, channel IDs, IP-derived attributes, or other recurring identifiers with each video record, the service enables records across uploads or accesses to be linked to the same individual or household.
assumptions: The metadata schema contains stable identifiers or quasi-identifiers reused across multiple records.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subnode id for this linkability case is inferred from standard linkability threat-tree structure.

title: Persistent storage enables detectability of a person's presence or activity
description: Once video metadata and files are stored in the database, the existence of records can allow an observer with access to the datastore or its indexes to detect that a particular person, account, device, or event is present in the system, even without reading full content.
assumptions: The datastore structure, indexes, filenames, or metadata fields expose enough signals to test whether a person or event is represented.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id is inferred; detectability applicability depends on whether datastore access or side channels exist.

title: Stored video records may be used beyond the user's expected purpose
description: After receipt, the datastore may retain metadata and files for analytics, moderation training, profiling, or other secondary uses not apparent from the immediate upload/store operation, making the eventual use of the data insufficiently transparent to data subjects.
assumptions: The stored data can later be queried or repurposed for secondary processing beyond the primary video-management function.
uncertainty_note: This is a plausible unawareness threat at the destination, but exact downstream uses are not described in the flow.

title: Retention of video metadata/files may exceed consented or expected scope
description: If the database keeps video metadata or files longer than consented to, or stores categories of metadata/files not covered by the user's consent or another valid legal basis, the receipt and storage at the datastore create a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Consent, contract, or other legal basis imposes limits on what video-related personal data may be stored and for how long.
uncertainty_note: Exact non-compliance subnode id is inferred; applicability depends on the system's legal basis, retention policy, and notices.

title: Excessive retention of child search and watch history
description: The destination data store receives and stores detailed child search and watch history, which is highly revealing behavioral data. If DS2 stores more history than is strictly necessary, or retains it longer than needed for the service purpose, this creates an avoidable disclosure of personal data through over-collection and over-retention.
assumptions: Assumes the collection contains identifiable or reasonably linkable child-level history records rather than only short-lived aggregated telemetry.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best-fit LINDDUN Pro judgment for unnecessary storage/retention as a form of avoidable data disclosure; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Stored history enables linking of a child's activities across sessions
description: Persisting search and watch history in a single childprofiles collection can allow records from multiple sessions, devices, or time periods to be linked to the same child profile. This enables construction of a longitudinal behavioral profile beyond what may be necessary for the immediate function.
assumptions: Assumes records are stored with a stable child/profile identifier or other persistent key enabling correlation over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subnode may differ depending on the threat-tree edition; this is a best-fit linking/correlation node.

title: Stored behavioral history may identify a child or household
description: Detailed search and watch history can act as a quasi-identifier. Even if direct identifiers are minimized, unique combinations of viewed content, search terms, timestamps, or device/account associations in DS2 may permit singling out or re-identification of the child or their household.
assumptions: Assumes history records include sufficiently granular events, timestamps, or associations to an account/device/profile.
uncertainty_note: Subnode is chosen as a best-fit identification threat; exact numbering may vary across LINDDUN Pro materials.

title: Behavioral history reveals sensitive interests and habits
description: Search and watch history can expose intimate preferences, routines, developmental traits, health-related interests, religious or cultural interests, or other sensitive aspects of a child. Storing this data in DS2 creates a detectability/inference risk because observers or downstream analytics can detect these traits from the stored records.
assumptions: Assumes the stored history is accessible to internal analytics, administrators, or downstream processes and contains semantically meaningful content choices.
uncertainty_note: This is a best-fit detectability/inference-style threat for sensitive traits inferred from stored behavior; exact tree-node numbering may differ.

title: Storage of child history may exceed user or parental expectations
description: Storing detailed child search and watch history in the child profile store may be unexpected or insufficiently transparent to the child or parent, especially if used for personalization, analytics, or long-term profiling. This creates a non-compliance risk with transparency, purpose-limitation, minimization, and child-data protection obligations.
assumptions: Assumes notice, consent/parental authorization, retention limits, and purpose specification are not clearly established for this storage activity.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on the actual legal basis, notices, and child-privacy controls in scope; exact subnode may vary.

title: Excessive disclosure in uploaded video content
description: The parent may upload videos that reveal more personal data than necessary for the approval purpose, such as the child's face, home interior, location clues, voices, or other bystanders. The act of sharing this rich media with the service creates a disclosure risk.
assumptions: The upload may contain personal data about the child, parent, and possibly third parties; the service's approval task may not require all visible/audible details.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on general LINDDUN disclosure categories; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Identification through video and transport metadata
description: The uploaded video and associated metadata in transit can directly or indirectly identify the parent, child, or household through faces, voices, filenames, device metadata, timestamps, IP-related context, or embedded geolocation.
assumptions: The upload flow carries the media file plus ordinary protocol/application metadata; metadata stripping may be incomplete or absent.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode may differ depending on whether the methodology separates content-based identification from metadata-based identification.

title: Linkability of uploads across sessions or accounts
description: Repeated uploads may be linkable via persistent identifiers, account identifiers, device/network metadata, or recurring visual/audio characteristics, allowing correlation of multiple submissions to the same family or child.
assumptions: The service uses authenticated or otherwise stable upload channels, or the media itself contains recurring identifiable patterns.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort node selection; exact linkability subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Over-collection and retention of uploaded video at the service
description: Upon receipt, the Video Management Service may store the full uploaded video and metadata for moderation, approval/rejection, analytics, troubleshooting, or future reuse beyond what is necessary for the stated purpose, exposing personal data of the child, parent, and third parties.
assumptions: P2 stores or processes uploads after receipt and may keep originals and metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; exact disclosure/over-processing subnode may differ in the local threat tree.

title: Secondary use of uploaded videos beyond approval/rejection
description: The destination process may use uploaded videos for purposes not expected by the parent, such as model training, staff performance review, content analytics, or product improvement, making the processing purpose unclear or broader than understood.
assumptions: The flow description states approval/rejection as the primary purpose; additional downstream uses are possible unless explicitly constrained.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode may vary; grounded in generic unawareness about hidden or expanded processing purposes.

title: Improper personal data management for uploaded child-related video
description: The service may fail to manage uploaded videos in a compliant manner, for example by lacking a lawful basis, inadequate parental notice, insufficient minimization, excessive retention, weak deletion handling, or inadequate protection for children's data during moderation and storage.
assumptions: The uploaded content concerns a child or family context and is therefore likely to require heightened governance and lifecycle controls.

title: Insufficient evidence of consent or submission terms for the upload
description: If the service does not record what the parent was told and agreed to at upload time, either party may later be unable to demonstrate whether the upload was authorized, what purpose applied, or whether approval/rejection criteria and data handling terms were accepted.
assumptions: The upload process may rely on click-through notices or implicit submission without robust evidence capture.

title: JWT in localStorage can act as a stable linkable identifier across browser contexts
description: Storing a JWT in browser localStorage makes the token persist client-side and accessible to scripts from the same origin. If the token contains a stable subject, session, or account identifier, repeated reads and reuse across visits or application components can link user actions and sessions together beyond what is necessary.

description: Browser localStorage is readable by any JavaScript executing in the same origin and may remain after the intended session ends. assumptions: Assumes same-origin scripts or local device access are plausible, and that the JWT grants access to personal data or itself contains personal data.

description: Storing the JWT in localStorage can create persistence that is not obvious to users.
